intro: A clavichord can alter a note after the finger has struck it. In this late fantasia, Bach makes an instrument quiet enough for a private room speak in interruptions, pauses and sudden changes of register.
question: How can pauses shape a piece without a steady beat?

cues.title: Touch after the attack
cues.text: The clavichord’s metal tangents strike the strings and remain in contact while the keys are held. Changes of finger pressure can affect a sounding note. Listen for the relationship between attack, continuation and release, not only the succession of pitches.
cues.evidence: The source identifies Joan Benson playing clavichord. The note describes the instrument’s mechanism; it does not claim to detect a particular pressure effect in the recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Gestures gather and separate
cues.text: Through this passage, quicker groups of notes alternate with more separated gestures. Listen to the gaps between groups as punctuation rather than trying to impose one continuous pace.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks increase around 0:30–0:35, then become less frequent by 0:45. The analysis supports a change in activity, not a measured tempo change.

cues.title: A practical book
cues.text: Bach published the two parts of his Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments in 1753 and 1762. Ornamentation and accompaniment were subjects for written instruction as well as skills transmitted from player to player.
cues.evidence: The introduction to The Essential C.P.E. Bach, pp. xiv and xix, documents the treatise’s publication and contents. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Another gathering of motion
cues.text: Across this stretch, the groups become busier before falling back into more widely spaced notes. Follow the length of each gesture rather than expecting every phrase to occupy the same amount of time.
cues.evidence: The report detects more attacks around 2:30–2:45 than around 2:20–2:25, followed by a reduction around 2:55–3:10.

cues.title: Room around each note
cues.text: Through the quieter phrases, attend to the decay after an attack. The duration of the sounding note and the wait before the next gesture contribute separately to the pace.
cues.evidence: The report shows quieter, less densely articulated writing around 3:00–3:25 than around 2:30–2:45. It cannot establish a particular fingering or release.

cues.title: Punctuation before pulse
cues.text: Listen for the ends of gestures: a held note, a short flourish and a gap can mark different kinds of stopping point. A quiet ending to a phrase need not mean the whole piece is about to finish.
cues.evidence: This is an editorial listening suggestion for the fantasia’s recurring contrasts. The report places a relatively sparse, low-level passage around 4:10–4:25.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pressure, then a break
cues.text: In this stretch, a forceful passage is followed by a marked withdrawal. Compare the spacing of the attacks before and after it; the interruption changes the scale of the phrase.
cues.evidence: The highest five-second relative-level window occurs around 4:50, followed by a large drop and fewer detected attacks around 5:00.

cues.title: A quieter continuation
cues.text: The surrounding passage returns to quieter gestures after another brief rise. Listen for changes in the weight and spacing of notes rather than assuming that every increase starts a new section.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls substantially between 5:20 and 5:30 and remains comparatively low through 6:00. The detected change does not identify a formal boundary.

cues.title: Burney at the clavichord
cues.text: Charles Burney described Bach playing the clavichord in 1772 until nearly eleven at night. His account emphasises expression and variety of modulation as well as technique; it is a contemporary report, not evidence of how Benson plays this recording.
cues.evidence: The Essential C.P.E. Bach, p. xiv, quotes Burney’s 1775 travel account, volume 2, p. 269. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Activity and weight together
cues.text: Across this stretch, the gestures become both busier and stronger. Compare this combination with passages where only the spacing changes; greater activity and greater force are distinct effects.
cues.evidence: Relative level and detected attack density rise through approximately 7:05–7:30, before both fall around 7:40.

cues.title: No single speaking pace
cues.text: Keep following the sizes of the gestures as the piece alternates runs and separated notes. The fantasia’s continuity can come from contrast and response rather than an unbroken accompaniment pattern.
cues.evidence: This is a general listening prompt. The analysis records repeated changes in activity and relative level around 7:40–8:20, without establishing their score positions.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A crest without an ending
cues.text: A stronger phrase is followed by another withdrawal in this stretch. Listen to how quickly a local arrival can give way to room for the next gesture.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 8:55–9:00, then falls substantially by 9:10 as detected attacks become less frequent.

cues.title: Crowded notes, then space
cues.text: Through this passage, quick groups give way to more widely separated attacks. Treat the retreat as part of the phrase’s shape, not as an unrelated interruption.
cues.evidence: The report detects closely packed attacks around 9:25–9:35, followed by reduced activity and relative level around 9:45.

cues.title: A late keyboard work
cues.text: The F♯ minor Fantasia dates from 1787. Bach’s estate catalogue lists it at the end of a sequence of solo keyboard works reaching back to 1731: more than half a century of composition.
cues.evidence: The Essential C.P.E. Bach, p. xiv, describes the estate catalogue’s keyboard sequence and dates Wq 67 to 1787. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: A last busy passage
cues.text: In the closing stretch, another busy passage gives way to quieter, more widely spaced notes. Listen for the reduction in activity without expecting an immediate end.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks are closely packed around 11:20–11:30, then diminish markedly around 11:40–11:50. The report does not align the change to a score marking.

cues.title: Leave room for the decay
cues.text: Across the final passage, attend to the remaining resonance and the silence that follows. The recording continues after the last musical activity has subsided.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls sharply around 12:15–12:20; the report detects no sound in the final windows around 12:25–12:30.

transitions.title: The run gives way to speech
transitions.how: Bach breaks the continuity of quick keyboard figures with shorter, separated gestures. Instead of maintaining an accompaniment beneath a new melody, the clavichord must articulate both the speaking line and its pauses: a fresh bass or chordal attack begins another response. This is the free fantasia’s contrast between running notes and recitative-like writing, not a sonata transition into a securely announced second key. The gaps let the preceding harmony decay before the next gesture changes its direction.
transitions.evidence: The map places sparse discourse at 180 s. Detected attacks fall from 5.8–6.8 per second around 2:30–2:45 to 1.2–2.2 around 3:00–3:10, with a substantial level retreat. Wq 67’s written alternation of passagework and recitative-like gestures supplies the structural context. No local chord or key is assigned: the clavichord chroma and form matches are unreliable.

transitions.title: A response replaces the outburst
transitions.how: The forceful gesture is answered by quieter, more widely separated clavichord attacks. Bach joins these states by interruption rather than by an orchestral-style crescendo or a continuous bass pattern: the listener has to retain the last harmony through its decay. Short melodic figures resume the discourse without restoring a regular accompaniment. On this instrument the change is one of touch, duration and spacing within a single keyboard sound, not a handover to a new instrumental colour.
transitions.evidence: The quiet episode begins at the map’s 322 s boundary, matching the report’s 5:22 structural change. Relative level falls from −15.1 dB at 5:20 to −35.6 dB at 5:30, when detected attacks are sparse. The score’s rhetorical alternation supports the description; no unaligned tempo marking, cadence type or local key is claimed.

transitions.title: Quick figures leave isolated sounds
transitions.how: In the final contrast, the rapid groups stop replenishing the sound and leave longer spaces around the remaining notes. The keyboard texture loses its running surface; individual melodic and bass attacks become audible as separate events. Bach’s free phrasing makes the approach to the end a reduction of activity rather than a mechanically repeated closing formula. The clavichord’s short decay matters here: the pauses increasingly separate the gestures instead of being filled by continuous resonance.
transitions.evidence: Closing withdrawal is mapped at 698 s, the report’s 11:38 change. Attack density drops from 6.4–6.6 per second at 11:20–11:30 to 0.8–1.4 at 11:40–11:50. The score’s free keyboard discourse supplies the context, but its closing bars are not aligned and the audio pitch estimates do not justify a named cadence here.

composer.background:
Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach. He was born in Weimar in 1714; Georg Philipp Telemann was one of his godfathers. The family moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, where his father became Thomaskantor. Emanuel learned the keyboard and composition at home, then studied law at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder. He made music his profession: by 1738 he had entered the circle of the Prussian crown prince Frederick, who became king in 1740.

Frederick played the flute, composed and maintained an orchestra whose leading musicians included Johann Joachim Quantz and the brothers Graun. Bach’s employment was chiefly as a keyboard accompanist. In his own publications he pursued a style independent of the king’s Italianate melodic preferences. His six ‘Prussian’ keyboard sonatas of 1742 and six ‘Württemberg’ sonatas of 1744 put contrasting textures, unexpected rests and highly ornamented slow movements inside the three-movement sonata. The player had to manage changes of character as precisely as changes of fingering.
composer.epithet: A keyboard player who made hesitation, interruption and a change of mind into musical form.
